chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutawakkil (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Sa'd Abadi narrated to us. He said: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah al-Barqi narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani narrated to us, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Munqari, from Hammad ibn Isa, from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) who said:

Among that which Luqman advised his son Natan is that he said to him: O my son! Let that with which you arm yourself against your enemy, so as to overcome him, be kind treatment and voicing your acceptance of him. Do not confront him with avoidance, lest what is in your soul becomes apparent to him and he prepares against you.

O my son! Fear God with such a fear that if you were to come to Him with the goodness of the two heavyweights (humans and jinn), you would still fear that God would punish you. And hope in God with such a hope that if you were to come to Him with the sins of the two heavyweights, you would still hope that God would forgive you.

O my son! I have carried boulders, iron, and every heavy load, but I have not carried anything heavier than an evil neighbour. And I have tasted every bitterness, but I have not tasted anything more bitter than poverty.

key_terms.الثقلين: The two heavyweights — refers to humans and jinn, the two accountable creations
key_terms.الفقر: Poverty — considered the bitterest of all afflictions
key_terms.المماسحة: Kind treatment, courtesy, amicable dealings — a strategy of disarming opponents through graciousness
key_terms.جار السوء: Evil neighbour — a proverbial expression for an unbearable burden

ai.seo_question: What did Luqman advise his son about dealing with enemies and fearing God?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transmits the wise counsel of Luqman to his son Natan, covering three themes: dealing with enemies through kindness rather than hostility, maintaining a perfect balance between fear of God's punishment and hope in His mercy, and reflections on the unmatched burdens of an evil neighbour and poverty. This advice, attributed to the Quranic sage Luqman, was delivered in the context of paternal counsel and was highly valued in the Shia tradition for combining practical social wisdom with profound theological insight.

en.bilal-muhammad: Muhammad b. Musa b. al-Mutawakkil (ra) narrated to us. He said: `Ali b. al-Husayn al-Sa`d Abadi narrated to us. He said: Ahmad b. Abi `Abdillah al-Barqi narrated to us. He said: `Ali b. Muhammad al-Qasani narrated to us from Sulayman b. Dawud al-Munqari from Hammad b. `Isa from al-Sadiq Ja`far b. Muhammad (as). He said:

Among that which Luqman advised his son Natan is that he said to him: O son! Arm yourself against your opponent with kind words and voicing your acceptance of him. Do not abandon him out of fear, or he will prepare to fight you.

O son! Fear Allah in such a way that if you had the goodness of the two heavyweights (humans and Jinn), you would still fear Allah’s punishment. Put your hope in Allah in such a way that if you had the sins of the two heavyweights, you would still hope for Allah’s forgiveness.

O son! I have carried boulders, iron, and every heavy thing, but I have not borne anything heavier than an evil neighbour. I have tasted every bitterness, but I have not tasted anything more bitter than poverty.
